newsitem.title: GERMANY: Berlin mayor ready to talk in Gestapo museum row.
newsitem.headline: Berlin mayor ready to talk in Gestapo museum row.

text.p: The mayor of Berlin, under fire for deciding against plans to build a museum about Nazi terror on the site of the Gestapo's headquarters, signalled on Wednesday he was ready to seek a compromise with his critics.
A Berlin government spokesman said Mayor Eberhard Diepgen would meet senior officials from the city's main political parties when he returns next week from a trip to Japan.

Diepgen's reaction followed widespread outrage, particularly among German and international Jewish leaders, over a decision by the city-state's government to postpone construction of the museum because of a lack of funds.

The protests prompted the parliamentary groups in Diepgen's ruling coalition to announce on Tuesday that they wanted the cash-strapped city to find other ways of making budget cuts and ensure the project goes ahead as planned.
Ignatz Bubis, the leader of Germany's Jewish community, welcomed the moves to get the museum built but said he wished that Diepgen's Christian Democrats (CDU) in Berlin, had been more enthusiastic.
"I would have preferred it if the CDU had seen the case for construction on its own merits," he told the Tageszeitung daily in an interview released ahead of publication on Thursday.

The museum, on a grassy wasteland in central Berlin where both Gestapo and SS headquarters once stood, was due to be finished for the 60th anniversary of the Kristallnacht pogroms, when Nazi mobs destroyed Jewish homes and businesses on November 9, 1938.
A temporary exhibition detailing some of the horrors of Nazi terror currently occupies part of the site, which borders one of the last remaining segments of the Berlin Wall.
